stem:
A 43-year-old man is evaluated for occasional, sudden-onset palpitations.  The patient has no history of heart disease, and family history is unremarkable.  After initial evaluation, he is treated with verapamil and reports marked improvement in the frequency of palpitation episodes.  The tracing below shows the electrical activity of a specific type of cardiac cell in the patient's heart.

Which of the following effects would verapamil administration most likely have on these cells?​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​
explanation:
The tracing shows the action potential of pacemaker cells in cardiac slow-response tissues such as the sinoatrial (SA) and atrioventricular (AV) nodes.  The pacemaker action potential includes the following phases:

  • Phase 4 (spontaneous depolarization) begins after hyperpolarization triggers the opening of nonselective cation channels that allow slow influx of Na+ ("funny current").  T-type (transient) Ca2+ channels then open once the membrane potential becomes more positive, allowing Ca2+ influx to contribute to depolarization.  As the pacemaker cell approaches threshold during late phase 4, L-type (long-lasting) Ca2+ channels begin to open, which further increases Ca2+ influx and helps the membrane reach threshold.

  • Phase 0 (upstroke) is characterized by continued opening of L-type Ca2+ channels.  In cardiac slow-response tissues, the action potential upstroke is much slower than in fast-response tissues (eg, ventricular myocytes, Purkinje fibers) and transitions gradually from phase 4 due to the relatively slow influx of Ca2+ into the cell (rather than rapid influx of Na+).

  • Phase 3 (repolarization) is characterized by the opening of K+ channels and efflux of K+ from the cell in conjunction with the closure of L-type Ca2+ channels.

This patient's sudden-onset palpitations are consistent with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT).  Class IV antiarrhythmics (eg, verapamil, diltiazem) are commonly used to treat supraventricular tachyarrhythmias such as PSVT.  They work by blocking L-type calcium channels in cardiac slow-response tissues.  Although L-type channels are best known for generating the phase 0 upstroke, they also open during late phase 4; therefore, blockade causes slowing of phase 4 depolarization and the phase 0 upstroke.  As a result, SA node firing and AV nodal conduction slow.  Class IV drugs also prolong the AV nodal refractory period.  Together, slowed AV nodal conduction and prolonged refractoriness interrupt the reentrant circuits responsible for most cases of PSVT.

(Choice A)  Verapamil decreases the amount of intracellular calcium available for excitation-contraction coupling within contractile cardiomyocytes.  This reduces myocardial contractility, which can be harmful in patients with impaired ventricular function.  However, the tracing shown in the question stem corresponds to a pacemaker action potential; pacemaker cells are specialized cardiomyocytes that contain few myofibrils and contribute minimally to contraction.

(Choices B and C)  Class I (sodium channel blockers) and class IV (calcium channel blockers) antiarrhythmics generally raise the threshold potential of fast- and slow-response tissues, respectively; with fewer channels available, greater depolarization is required to generate enough inward current to trigger an action potential.  Channel blockade also reduces action potential amplitude and upstroke velocity, slowing impulse conduction within the respective tissues.

(Choice D)  Verapamil increases, rather than reduces, the refractory period of nodal tissue because it slows the recovery of L-type calcium channels from inactivation; as a result, nodal cells remain refractory even after repolarization is complete.  Class IA (eg, quinidine) and class III (eg, amiodarone) antiarrhythmics also increase the refractory period but do so by blocking potassium channels and prolonging repolarization.

Educational objective:Class IV antiarrhythmics (eg, verapamil, diltiazem) are commonly used to treat supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.  They work by blocking L-type calcium channels in slow-response cardiac tissues, slowing late phase 4 (spontaneous depolarization) and phase 0 (upstroke).  This decreases the sinoatrial node firing rate, slows atrioventricular nodal conduction, and prolongs atrioventricular nodal refractoriness.​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​
